title: Transformational marketing: From demand creation to demand stewardship
summary: Transformational marketing: From demand creation to demand stewardship Part of a new four-part series, this introductory article explores how the functional levels of business must transform to implement sustainable strategic management. In
content: Transformational marketing: From demand creation to demand stewardship Part of a new four-part series, this introductory article explores how the functional levels of business must transform to implement sustainable strategic management. In our previous series, we argued that business education was at the crossroads. We made the case for sustainable strategic management, demonstrated flourishing circularity, and traced the shape of the polycrisis demanding response. The transformation we called for is not cosmetic, and it cannot be achieved by technique alone. It requires a deeper shift in how business leaders perceive reality – a shift in consciousness. This series takes up the parallel work: showing what transformation looks like in the firm’s functional architecture once that shift has begun.

title: Editorial: The grey side of the blue bioeconomy: assessing unreported transactions and financial drainage in blue bioeconomy sectors
summary: The blue bioeconomy has become a central pillar of sustainable development for coastal nations (Lees et al., 2025), contributing directly to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN, 2016;Vieira et al., 2020). Its gro
content: The blue bioeconomy has become a central pillar of sustainable development for coastal nations (Lees et al., 2025), contributing directly to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN, 2016;Vieira et al., 2020). Its growing importance is reflected in strategic policy frameworks adopted by major economies, including the European Union (EC, 2025) and China (Zhang et al., 2022), which envision a future driven by biotechnology, innovation, sustainable resource use, and effective governance. Despite this momentum, research has largely focused on the opportunities offered by the blue bioeconomy, while its "grey side", namely the informal, unreported, and poorly regulated activities that undermine environmental sustainability, economic performance, and governance has warranted relatively little attention. This apparent imbalance is also visible in the scientific literature.Using equivalent targeted queries in the Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection (Clarivate) (see Appendix), we identified only eleven publications (ten original research articles and one review article) addressing themes at the intersection of the blue bioeconomy and its proposed "grey side", published between 2016 and 2026 -see the full dataset at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21285844. This relatively underexplored research area comprises 41 authors, with an international co-authorship rate of 27.27%. The eleven publications have received 193 citations, with nearly 80% accounted for by the three most highly cited articles 1 . Excluding the review article, which adopts a global perspective, the remaining ten empirical studies were conducted across Southeast Asia (Indonesia, n = 2; Vietnam, n = 2), the Americas (Mexico, n = 2; Brazil, n = 1), South Asia (India, n = 1), the Middle East (Saudi Arabia, n = 1), and Africa (Cameroon, n = 1). Although no clear temporal growth trend is evident over the ten-year study period, the thematic map (Figure 1) reveals the emergence of distinct research domains within this developing field.[Please insert Figure 1 Collectively, the studies of this Research Topic demonstrate that addressing the 'grey economy' within the blue bioeconomy sector is fundamental to achieving sustainable development. Strengthening transparency, governance, and institutional capacity while reducing unreported activities and financial leakages will be essential to ensure that blue bioeconomy policies deliver lasting environmental, economic, and social benefits. By bringing these often-overlooked dimensions into focus, this collection contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges and opportunities that will shape the future of the global blue bioeconomy.

title: Mapping rural livelihood strategies in China using deep learning
summary: Rural livelihood strategies significantly influence socio-ecological systems and sustainability outcomes. However, spatially explicit data on livelihood compositions remain scarce at national scales. We developed a Deep Rural Livelihood Mod
content: Rural livelihood strategies significantly influence socio-ecological systems and sustainability outcomes. However, spatially explicit data on livelihood compositions remain scarce at national scales. We developed a Deep Rural Livelihood Model (DRLM) combining satellite imagery (Landsat, VIIRS) with household survey data to map four livelihood strategy probabilities across rural China in 2020: farming-only (F), farming-dominated mixed (F_NF), non-farming-dominated mixed (NF_F), and non-farming-only (NF). Using quantile-regression XGBoost, we expanded survey-derived labels from 283 rural observation sites to 38,306 rural settlements and trained a dual-branch ResNet architecture with Dirichlet regression. Agreement with the expanded settlement-level labels was high, whereas independent validation against actual survey data showed moderate performance, with stronger support for dominant livelihood categories than for mixed categories. This dataset provides settlement-scale probabilistic information to support analyses of rural transformation, sustainability-related indicators, and socio-ecological change.

title: The impacts of large-scale farming, refugees and resettlement on land use land cover changes and ecosystems services values in Abobo Woreda, Gambella Regional State, Ethiopia
summary: Resettlement programs, refugee settlements, and large-scale agricultural farming are major drivers of the increasing frequency and intensity of environmental degradation. This study aimed to assess the impacts of large-scale agriculture, re
content: Resettlement programs, refugee settlements, and large-scale agricultural farming are major drivers of the increasing frequency and intensity of environmental degradation. This study aimed to assess the impacts of large-scale agriculture, refugee settlements, and resettlement on land use/land cover (LULC) change and ecosystem service values and functions in Abobo Wereda. The study adopted a sequential explanatory research design. First, maximum likelihood supervised classification techniques were applied to Landsat images acquired in 1987, 2006, and 2025 to generate LULC maps, which were validated through field observations. ERDAS Imagine 2015, ArcGIS 10.7, and SPSS version 20 were used for image processing, spatial analysis, and statistical analysis, respectively. Subsequently, household survey data were collected from 292 proportionally distributed households across four menders. An integrated valuation approach, tailored to Ethiopian conditions, was applied to estimate ecosystem service values (ESVs) and functions in relation to land use and land cover (LULC) changes between 1987 and 2025 in the study area. To evaluate the reliability of this estimation process, the Coefficient of Sensitivity (CS) was employed, using LULC classes as proxies for their corresponding biomes. The results identified seven LULC categories: forestland, wetland, woodland, farmland, bare land, water bodies, and grassland. Between 1987 and 2006, forestland, grassland, and woodland declined at annual rates of 0.51 ha, 1.47 ha, and 2.84 ha, respectively, while farmland and bare land expanded at rates of 37.3 ha and 9.50 ha per year. From 2006 to 2025, the expansion of bare land and farmland continued, with mean annual increases of 859.43 ha and 9.88 ha, respectively. In contrast, forestland and grassland decreased at rates of 1.27 ha and 10 ha per year, respectively. Overall, the LULC trend over the entire study period indicates substantial land cover degradation, largely driven by large-scale agricultural expansion, refugee settlements, and resettlement activities. Changes in LULC were accompanied by shifts in ESVs. Between 1987 and 2006, the ESVs of natural forests, woodland, and grassland declined, whereas those of wetlands, water bodies, and farmland increased. Conversely, from 2006 to 2025, the ESVs of natural forests, wetlands, water bodies, and grasslands decreased, while farmland and woodland ESVs increased, mainly due to farmland expansion and settlement pressures. At the level of individual ecosystem functions, most services showed declining trends, except for water supply (1987–2006) and food production (2006–2025).The findings suggest that sustainable land management in Abobo Wereda requires an integrated approach that balances large-scale agricultural investments, refugee settlement, and resettlement programs with ecosystem conservation. title: Applying Mycelium-Based Materials in Real-World Contexts: The MUSE - MyceliUm SEat Framework
summary: Abstract This paper presents the MUSE - MyceliUm SEat framework as a research-through-design approach for applying mycelium-based materials in real-world contexts. Addressing the gap between experimental biomaterial research and functional
content: Abstract This paper presents the MUSE - MyceliUm SEat framework as a research-through-design approach for applying mycelium-based materials in real-world contexts. Addressing the gap between experimental biomaterial research and functional deployment, the project establishes a cross-scale methodology that moves from extreme performance testing to interior spatial integration. Phase I situates mycelium composites within a high-performance racing environment to accelerate material optimisation under strict structural and ergonomic constraints. Insights from systematic material testing are consolidated into a material matrix adaptable to diverse functional requirements. Phase II translates this knowledge into furniture-scale applications, employing varied fabrication strategies and reciprocal material-form development. The “Living” Room installation functions as a long-term public testbed, enabling evaluation of performance, perception, and ageing under real use conditions. The framework demonstrates how extreme scenarios, interdisciplinary collaboration, and spatial deployment can advance living materials beyond demonstrators toward scalable biodesign practice.

title: Evolving circular pedagogy: a framework for immersive transdisciplinary learning
summary: The contemporary world is undergoing profound socio-economic and environmental transformations that necessitate a radical re-evaluation of how we learn, teach, innovate and engage with research. Traditional educational models are increasing
content: The contemporary world is undergoing profound socio-economic and environmental transformations that necessitate a radical re-evaluation of how we learn, teach, innovate and engage with research. Traditional educational models are increasingly insufficient to address the complexity of the twin transition (i.e. green and digital), in which countries need to identify the most effective strategies to advance the digital and green transformations necessary to support sustainable development. Educational systems and frameworks also need to respond to the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its three pillars: environment, society, and economy. This research study offers critical insights into the need to build an actionable framework that supports the development of innovative learning spaces and pedagogies within an Immersive Transdisciplinary Learning framework better attuned to the realities of contemporary society. We propose an innovative approach that integrates immersive technologies, transdisciplinary collaboration, and real-world applications to reshape knowledge exchange processes as the learning loop continues to evolve through the lens of Circular Pedagogy.

title: SUSTAINABILITY AS A CATALYST FOR INDUSTRIAL GROWTH: ASSESSING GREEN MANUFACTURING PRACTICES IN EDO NORTH, EDO STATE, NIGERIA
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Manufacturing firms in Nigeria face mounting pressure from rising energy costs, environmental regulations, and global demand for sustainability. This study qualitatively investigates how GMPs influence the growth trajectories of manufacturi
content: Manufacturing firms in Nigeria face mounting pressure from rising energy costs, environmental regulations, and global demand for sustainability. This study qualitatively investigates how GMPs influence the growth trajectories of manufacturing firms in Edo North, Edo State, Nigeria. Multiple case studies of 24 firms across lime stone and cement manufacturing, agro-processing, food processing, quarrying, sawmilling, fish processing, light fabrication, and packaging, among others, are used. Data were collected through interviews with firm leaders, site observations, and document reviews between September 2025 and March 2026. Green manufacturing practices serve as significant catalysts for firm growth in Edo North by reducing operational costs, improving quality, gaining regulatory and reputational benefits, and opening new market opportunities. However, the study concludes that the benefits of adopting green manufacturing are not evenly realized, largely because of contextual constraints in infrastructure, finance, technical capacity and regulatory environments. The government at all levels, especially the Edo State government, should provide tax rebates and low-interest green loans to manufacturers adopting energy-efficient machinery and renewable energy systems

title: Salivary Biomarkers in the Diagnosis of Periodontal Diseases: From Screening to Personalized Therapy
summary: Periodontal diseases comprise a heterogeneous group of biofilm-associated inflammatory conditions ranging from reversible plaque-induced gingivitis to progressive periodontitis with destruction of the periodontal ligament, cementum, and alv
content: Periodontal diseases comprise a heterogeneous group of biofilm-associated inflammatory conditions ranging from reversible plaque-induced gingivitis to progressive periodontitis with destruction of the periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone. Conventional diagnosis relies on clinical and radiographic measures that primarily document accumulated tissue damage rather than ongoing molecular activity. Saliva has emerged as an attractive diagnostic medium because it can be collected repeatedly, non-invasively, and at relatively low cost while containing microbial products, inflammatory mediators, tissue-degradation enzymes, bone-remodelling molecules, nucleic acids, metabolites, and proteins derived from periodontal tissues and gingival crevicular fluid. Research has identified matrix metalloproteinase-8, interleukin-1β, interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor-α, macrophage inflammatory protein-1α, calprotectin, receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand, osteoprotegerin, haemoglobin, selected periodontal pathogens, and multi-omics signatures as promising candidate biomarkers. However, diagnostic performance varies substantially among studies because of differences in periodontal case definitions, saliva collection protocols, analytical platforms, disease severity, systemic comorbidities, smoking exposure, age, medication use, and statistical modelling. This narrative review examines the biological basis, analytical characteristics, and clinical applications of salivary biomarkers in periodontal diseases. Particular attention is given to their potential roles in population screening, differentiation of periodontal health, gingivitis, and periodontitis, identification of active tissue destruction, assessment of progression risk, monitoring of treatment response, and selection of personalized preventive or therapeutic strategies. Evidence supporting single biomarkers is compared with that for composite host–microbial panels, proteomic, metabolomic, transcriptomic, and microbiome-based approaches. Current findings indicate that salivary testing is most appropriately considered an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, comprehensive periodontal examination. Translation into routine care will require standardized pre-analytical procedures, externally validated thresholds, prospective studies with clinically relevant outcomes, assessment in medically diverse populations, and development of affordable point-of-care technologies. Properly validated salivary biomarker panels could ultimately shift periodontal care from retrospective documentation of tissue loss toward biologically informed screening, risk stratification, and longitudinal disease management. https://doi.org/10.52783/jchr.v16.i4.15783

title: Effect of different manure application rates on the nutritional composition of yam landraces grown under field conditions in Southern Ethiopia
summary: Yam is an important tuber crop for food security, income, and medicinal use globally. Its productivity and nutritional quality vary among species and are influenced by agronomic practices such as manure application. This study evaluated the
content: Yam is an important tuber crop for food security, income, and medicinal use globally. Its productivity and nutritional quality vary among species and are influenced by agronomic practices such as manure application. This study evaluated the effect of different manure rates on the nutritional composition of six yam landraces under field conditions in Ethiopia from 2023 to 2024. A Randomized Complete Block Design was used with five treatments: control (0 tons/ha), T 1 (10 tons/ha), T 2 (20 tons/ha), T 3 (30 tons/ha), and T 4 (40 tons/ha) of manure, each replicated three times. Proximate analyses (protein, fiber, ash, fat, carbohydrate, and energy) were conducted, and data were analyzed using two-way ANOVA, with mean separation by Tukey’s HSD at p < 0.05. Results showed significant differences ( p < 0.05) in nutritional composition among manure treatments and landraces. Protein content increased with higher manure rates, indicating a significant interaction between manure application and yam landraces proximate composition. Overall, moderate manure rates; T2 (20 tons/ha) to T 3 (30 tons/ha) produced the highest nutritional values. Specifically, Duurundufa, Gebsh, Afri, Ayno, and Qekila recorded highest values for protein (6.75%), fat (3.20%), fiber (7.30%), ash (5.30%), and carbohydrate (72.0%), respectively. These five landraces are recommended for breeding and germplasm conservation due to their superior nutritional profiles and low fat level. Organic manure improved protein content in tuber crops, which are typically high in carbohydrates but low in protein, a critical nutrient in resource-limited regions like Ethiopia. The findings support sustainable manure management to enhance yam productivity and nutritional quality. However, variation among landraces suggests the need for further research across diverse agro-ecologies to optimize manure rates and improve nutritional outcomes in future research settings recommended.

title: Biodesigning in a Different Patch: Place, Scale and Regenerative Materialities
summary: Abstract From unceded Australian Country and neighbouring regions, this paper investigates biodesign as a situated, multi-scalar practice, attentive to place, material ecologies, and more‑than‑human relations, reporting from a different ‘pa
content: Abstract From unceded Australian Country and neighbouring regions, this paper investigates biodesign as a situated, multi-scalar practice, attentive to place, material ecologies, and more‑than‑human relations, reporting from a different ‘patch’ to the dominant centre. Drawing on deep‑time Indigenous knowledge systems and emerging biotechnological practices, it contributes a relational, place‑responsive orientation for biodesign, extending its conceptual, ethical, and methodological possibilities. Through auto-ethnographic reflection and case studies spanning Indigenous-led practices, biomaterials research, and regenerative infrastructures, it reveals how biodesign is enacted differently when grounded in specific bioregional, cultural, and material conditions. The practices discussed in the paper demonstrate a bioinclusive aesthetic – embracing growth, decay, contamination, and microbial co‑habitation as regenerative design forces for shaping multispecies futures. Reframing biodesign in this way, as a pluriversal and multi-scalar activity, this study puts forward a set of principles for multi-scalar biodesign that foreground locality, relationality and responsibility when designing with living systems.

title: Tamarind Value Chains for Small-Scale Producers: A Review of Opportunities, Challenges, and Development Pathways
summary: Abstract Tamarind ( Tamarindus indica ) is a multipurpose tree that thrives in arid and semi-arid regions worldwide and supports rural livelihoods through its ecological, economic, and cultural importance. Beyond contributing to household s
content: Abstract Tamarind ( Tamarindus indica ) is a multipurpose tree that thrives in arid and semi-arid regions worldwide and supports rural livelihoods through its ecological, economic, and cultural importance. Beyond contributing to household subsistence and income generation, tamarind products are used in traditional medicine and culinary practices, and sold in local markets. However, its market potential for small-scale producers remains underexplored. This review synthesizes evidence from 32 empirical studies, limited to those published in English between 2000 and 2024, to examine how Indigenous, traditional, and local knowledge, together with value chain dynamics, shape market opportunities for producers. The findings describe how traditional knowledge underpins the widespread use, management, and conservation of tamarind. Nevertheless, market integration is constrained by low species regeneration rates, limited processing and value-addition capacity, weak market linkages, and producers’ limited access to the end market relative to downstream intermediaries. The reviewed studies suggest that realizing tamarind’s potential as a sustainable income-generating product requires interventions that build on Indigenous, traditional, and local knowledge while improving silvicultural practices, strengthening value addition, and expanding equitable market access. Coordinated efforts among policymakers, researchers, extension services, and producers are essential to ensure that increased market participation translates into sustainable socioeconomic benefits for rural communities while supporting long-term resource management.

title: A global comparison of net-zero carbon building practices
summary: Despite extensive research on individual net-zero carbon building (NZCB) practices, prior studies fail to systematically map global adoption patterns across diverse regulatory and market contexts. This study addresses this gap by investigat
content: Despite extensive research on individual net-zero carbon building (NZCB) practices, prior studies fail to systematically map global adoption patterns across diverse regulatory and market contexts. This study addresses this gap by investigating current NZCB practices worldwide. A comprehensive list of global NZCB practices, with associated enablers and barriers, was first identified through a literature review. A global survey was then employed to explore the practical adoption of the practices. Six countries/ regions participated in the survey: Australia, New Zealand, Italy, South Africa, Sri Lanka and Hong Kong. Survey data were analysed using descriptive and frequency analysis. The study identifies three empirically derived adoption patterns: common, varied, and low across countries/regions. Use of solar photovoltaics, energy-efficient HVAC and modular systems were found to be commonly adopted, while advanced technologies like carbon-infused materials were least adopted. Lack of direct financial incentives emerged as the key global barrier, while robust government policies were the main enabler for NZCB adoption worldwide. These findings provide empirical benchmarks for cross-country NZCB adoption and actionable strategies to accelerate low-adoption practices globally.

title: Public versus stakeholder engagement: A distinction for policy-makers to avoid undue interference
source: South African Journal on Human Rights
summary: This paper examines the role of public participation in policy-making, with a focus on public health interventions in South Africa. Public participation processes are crucial for ensuring policies reflect the public good and incorporate the
content: This paper examines the role of public participation in policy-making, with a focus on public health interventions in South Africa. Public participation processes are crucial for ensuring policies reflect the public good and incorporate the lived experiences of diverse communities to develop effective and responsive solutions. However, improper implementation can alienate segments of the population, erode trust and undermine the legitimacy of policy decisions. This paper highlights the concern that participatory processes are often skewed towards powerful stakeholders, such as corporate entities, rather than vulnerable groups who are most in need of public health policies. After delving into the nature of public participation in policy-making processes in South Africa, where and how these processes fall short, as well as how these processes are abused, this paper concludes with suggestions on how participation can be strengthened to reflect the public good.

title: Understanding and Reporting PFAS Exposure: Wide-Scope Retrospective Suspect Screening of High-Resolution Mass Spectrometry Data from Exposomics Studies
summary: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) comprise thousands of persistent and structurally diverse chemicals that contribute to chronic human exposure. Yet, routine biomonitoring targets
content: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) comprise thousands of persistent and structurally diverse chemicals that contribute to chronic human exposure. Yet, routine biomonitoring targets only a limited set of regulated legacy compounds, underestimating overall exposure. We present a retrospective, wide-scope suspect screening analysis framework to extract PFAS information from archived LC–HRMS exposomics datasets. A curated list of 1,666 PFAS, filtered for reversed-phase LC compatibility and enriched with structural descriptors, predicted retention indices, and MS 2 fragments, was used to reprocess two human biomonitoring studies involving firefighter serum pools and population-based plasma samples. Candidate features were prioritized using precursor accuracy, isotopic patterns, and MS 2 similarity, followed by spectral quality filtering and retention time-index regression models based on isotopically labeled standards, reinforcing identification confidence. The reanalysis recovered up to 80% of previously reported PFAS while revealing overlooked high-confidence carboxylic, sulfonic, and sulfonamidoacetic acid homologues, and >30 tentative PFAS series, encompassing isomeric clusters (alcohols and ethers) and structurally distinct subclasses (alkylpyrimidine PFAS). The reanalysis framework also revealed shared homologue patterns across exposure contexts. By framing PFAS chemical space and providing a reusable repository of confirmed and tentative structures, this framework reinterprets HRMS biobanked data, improving PFAS pattern assessment.

title: Coordination regimes, treaty layering and governance congestion in global biodiversity governance: The International Big Cat Alliance
summary: Global biodiversity governance has expanded into a dense regime complex of overlapping institutions, generating risks of fragmentation and coordination challenges. In response, governance arrangements increasingly emphasise coordination acr
content: Global biodiversity governance has expanded into a dense regime complex of overlapping institutions, generating risks of fragmentation and coordination challenges. In response, governance arrangements increasingly emphasise coordination across existing frameworks, yet their systemic implications remain under-examined. This paper develops the concept of coordination-oriented meta-regimes as an analytical lens to examine how treaty-based arrangements may reshape regime complexity. Using the International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA) as an exploratory case, this paper analyses its institutional architecture. The findings suggest that IBCA introduces additional organisational structures, reporting systems and financial channels within an already dense biodiversity governance landscape. This highlights how treaty-based coordination arrangements may contribute to institutional congestion and governance sclerosis through cumulative layering. Under certain conditions, these dynamics may generate governance congestion and institutional sclerosis, with fragmentation risks emerging as a secondary consequence.

title: Identifying strategies to improve the water productivity of permanent raised beds
source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
summary: Permanent raised bed (PRB) farming systems combine several elements (e.g. reduced tillage, controlled traffic, stubble retention) of conservation agriculture. PRB systems have recently been introduced into irrigated areas but there is a lac
content: Permanent raised bed (PRB) farming systems combine several elements (e.g. reduced tillage, controlled traffic, stubble retention) of conservation agriculture. PRB systems have recently been introduced into irrigated areas but there is a lack of information on the agronomic and irrigation performance of these systems under these conditions. Three years of field research into the performance of irrigated PRBs was conducted in south east Queensland, Australia and north west Pakistan. These studies benchmarked the irrigation performance of variously sized PRB systems and explored the impact of bed renovation method (no tillage (NT), shallow cultivation (SC) and blade ploughing (BP)) on soil hydro-physical properties (bulk density, soil moisture storage, infiltration), irrigation performance, crop yield and input water productivity (WP). Irrigation management strategies to improve lateral infiltration and irrigation performance were also investigated. The initial benchmarking study was conducted on two farms with clayey Vertisol (Australia) and three farms with sandy clay loam, Alfisol, (Pakistan) soils. The results showed low irrigation performance with excessive deep drainage potential. The irrigation application efficiency (Ea) on the clayey Vertisol and sandy clay loam was as low as 68% and 50%, requirement efficiency (Er) 96% and 77% and distribution uniformity (DU) 86% and 66%, respectively. However, the majority of the narrow beds (66 cm furrow spacing) were over-irrigated on the sandy clay loam while the wide beds (132 cm furrow spacing) were under-irrigated. Inappropriate renovation and bed furrow dimensions, sub-optimal irrigation management and poor lateral infiltration were the main factors likely to affect WP of irrigated PRBs. The evaluation of bed renovation methods found that BP on the clayey Vertisol reduced (~6%) the average seasonal bulk density of the surface 0-30 cm compared to the NT treatment. BP was found to produce higher lateral infiltration into the beds than either NT or SC. Freshly applied BP and SC produced a higher (~23%) cumulative infiltration than NT but the effect was transient and was not significant in the following season when the PRB renovation treatments were not freshly applied. The SC beds slump more than the BP and NT beds. The soil water content in the beds indicated that there was increased water storage associated with BP. PRB renovation (i.e. SC or BP) was found to reduce irrigation performance on the clayey Vertisol when the irrigation was farmer managed. The volume of irrigation water applied to the fresh SC and BP treatments increased by up 13% and 55%, and Ea was reduced by up to 9% and 29% respectively, compared with NT during the 2010 wheat and 2011 corn seasons. NT produced a higher wheat yield and WP, but the lower wheat yield in the cultivated treatments was associated with poor crop establishment from a rough soil surface and inadequate seeder performance in this season.
